# Compositing

A composite combines many burst products into one image per grid square.
`ResolutionWeighter` writes composites on the 10 km squares of the Military
Grid Reference System (MGRS), so results from different bursts, orbits and
dates line up pixel for pixel.

## Get the grid squares

`MGRSGrid` lists the grid squares that overlap an area. Its `resolution` is the
pixel size of the composite and must equal the `grid_spacing` the products were
processed with:

```{.python}
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import MGRSGrid

aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))
```

Each square is an `MGRSGeoBox`, which knows its MGRS code, its pixel grid and
its UTM zone, `square.crs`. Both classes come from
[freezebase](https://lqgentner.github.io/freezebase/), whose guide
[The MGRS grid](https://lqgentner.github.io/freezebase/user-guide/mgrs-grid.html)
explains the grid and why it suits composites.

The products must be in the zone of the square: process them with
`crs=square.crs` and keep the default `align_to_standard_grid=True`. A product
on a different grid is rejected.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not process products for a composite with `crs="auto"`

`"auto"` takes each burst's own zone, and a burst whose center lies in the
neighboring zone would be projected there, not in the zone of the square.
:::

[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd) shows the whole loop from
an area to the composites of its squares.

## Compose with local resolution weighting

Two methods combine all products that cover a square, whatever their orbit or
direction: `compose_rtc_lrw()` for backscatter and `compose_coherence_lrw()` for
coherence. Each pixel is weighted toward the acquisitions with the highest
spatial resolution at that pixel. This is called local resolution weighting
(LRW); [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains how it
works.

```{.python}
from s1bursts import ResolutionWeighter, TimeRange

weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
for square in squares:
    composite = weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(
        rtc.products, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window,
    )
```

The method returns the composite, a record whose file
`fm.get_product_path(composite)` holds the backscatter. Pass the `TimeRange` of
your search as `time_range`, so that every square records the same compositing
window.

The weights come from the RTC products, so `compose_coherence_lrw()` takes the
RTC products of the same dates as well:

```{.python}
coherence_composite = weighter.compose_coherence_lrw(
    coherence.products, rtc.products, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window,
)
```

## Quality layers

With `write_qa=True`, two quality layers are written beside an LRW composite:

- The number of observations (`QA-NUM`): how many acquisitions contributed to
  each pixel.
- The composite quality map (`QA-CQM`): how fine the combined detail of each
  pixel is.

The composite lists them in its `layers`, and `fm.open()` reads each layer's
file:

```{.python}
from s1bursts.product import Layer

with fm.open(composite, Layer.QA_CQM) as src:
    cqm = src.read(1)
```

## Composites per pass direction

Three more methods keep ascending and descending orbits apart:

| Method | Combines | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `compose_rtc_by_pass()` | RTC | Backscatter by viewing direction |
| `compose_gtc_by_pass()` | GTC | Backscatter without terrain flattening |
| `compose_coherence_by_pass()` | Coherence | Coherence by viewing direction |

They return a dictionary of composites keyed by pass direction, `"Ascending"`
and `"Descending"`. They take a plain average without resolution weights, and
their only quality layer is the number of observations.

## Choose how to combine

Every method uses `aggregation="mean"` by default. Pass `aggregation="median"`,
or a number between 0 and 1 for a quantile, to reduce the influence of
outliers.

Composites are written in linear units, like the products they combine.
Convert backscatter to decibels after reading it, as `10 * np.log10(gamma0)`,
so that the averaging has already happened on linear values.

All inputs of one call must share a polarization, the processing settings and
the SNAP version, the inputs of both pass directions included, and coherence
inputs must share a temporal baseline. A pass composite that already exists
must match the settings and SNAP version of the direction being added. A SNAP version that could not be
determined matches any. The RTC products that weight a coherence composite
must share their settings among themselves, and the DEM and SNAP version with
the coherence products; the composite records the settings of the coherence
products only.

Like processing, compositing skips a square whose files already exist, after
checking that they were made on the same grid and with the same settings. Pass
`overwrite=True` to replace composites made with other settings.
